discovery: Theoretical prediction and characterization of kilonovae, establishing neutron-star mergers as observable sites of r-process heavy-element nucleosynthesis

nominees.name: Li-Xin Li
nominees.affiliation: Kavli Institute for Astronomy and Astrophysics, Peking University

nominees.name: Daniel Kasen
nominees.affiliation: University of California, Berkeley and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory

motivation: The origin of the heaviest elements, from gold to uranium, was one of physics' great open questions. Li (with the late Paczynski) first predicted that radioactive decay of neutron-rich ejecta from compact-object mergers would power an optical transient. Metzger and collaborators computed self-consistently, with nuclear-network heating, how bright these 'kilonovae' would be and how long they would last. Kasen and collaborators showed that lanthanide opacities make r-process-rich ejecta glow red and infrared. These predictions guided the 2017 identification of the kilonova accompanying GW170817, the first direct observation of r-process nucleosynthesis at work. Their framework links nuclear physics, gravitational-wave astronomy and the chemical record preserved in the oldest metal-poor stars and ultra-faint dwarf galaxies. It turned decades of speculation about where the heavy elements are made into quantitative, data-driven science.
